title: Wendell and the Visitor
premise: Xanthe Dunmore's late-night call-in show becomes a conduit for the dead when listeners who died the previous week start phoning in, each asking him to remember things he never knew. The arrival of Wendell, his childhood imaginary friend, unchanged after forty years, forces Xanthe back to the summer of 1974, when a drowned boy named Toby Vance was erased from every memory, record, and photograph in the town of Harrow Bend. Wendell is not a friend but a warden of that erasure, and Xanthe, as the only person whose memory resisted, must return what was taken: Toby's name, spoken aloud by someone who loved him. As the dead callers multiply and the town's founders close in to protect their bargain with the thing beneath the reservoir, Xanthe discovers the final voice required is his own mother's — and she has been dead for eleven years. In the climax at the drowned church under the reservoir, Xanthe speaks Toby's name into the water, unmaking the town's prosperity and nearly himself; the resolution leaves Harrow Bend flooded with memory, Wendell dissolved into an ordinary man's grief, and Xanthe hosting one last show where the living finally call in.
about_author: Edmund Thackeray is the pen name of a former overnight radio engineer from the Ohio Valley who spent twenty years logging dead air and claims the quiet hours taught him everything he knows about what listens back. He writes horror rooted in small-town bargains, vanished children, and the machinery of forgetting.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: Third-person limited on Xanthe during his 2 a.m. broadcast, when a caller identifies herself as Marla Ketch, obituary printed four days ago, and asks him to remember a name he's never heard. He assumes a prank, but her voice carries the specific static of the station's own dead frequency. Emotional beat: professional skepticism curdling into unease.

chapters.title: The Man on the Porch
chapters.summary: Xanthe returns to his childhood home in Harrow Bend to settle his late mother's estate and finds Wendell waiting — exactly as he left him at age nine, down to the striped scarf. Wendell speaks casually of obligations dating to 1974. POV stays with Xanthe. Emotional beat: uncanny nostalgia turning to dread as he realizes no adult ever saw Wendell but him.

chapters.title: What the Town Owes
chapters.summary: Wendell explains the terms without explaining anything: something was taken in 1974, the town has prospered on the taking, and the debt is now due because the taker is dying. Xanthe demands specifics; Wendell offers only a riddle about water and names. Emotional beat: frustration and the first crack in Xanthe's disbelief.

chapters.title: Obituaries
chapters.summary: Back on air, Xanthe tests the phenomenon deliberately, reading names from last week's death notices; each deceased caller answers, and each mentions Toby Vance — a name absent from every archive. A second caller, still alive, begs him to stop. Emotional beat: vertigo as the impossible becomes repeatable, testable fact.

chapters.title: The Reservoir
chapters.summary: Xanthe walks the shoreline of Lake Meridian, built in 1974 over the old lowland district, and meets elderly councilman Aldous Prewitt, who warns him off with practiced warmth that doesn't reach his eyes. Underwater lights flicker in a pattern like Morse. Emotional beat: the sense of being watched by a whole town.

chapters.title: Mother's Tapes
chapters.summary: Sorting his mother's belongings, Xanthe finds reel-to-reel tapes labeled with dates from 1974 and one labeled TOBY — DO NOT PLAY. He plays it anyway: his mother's young voice mid-argument with someone about 'giving him back.' Emotional beat: grief complicated by betrayal; his mother knew.

chapters.title: Wendell's Patience Wears Thin
chapters.summary: Confronted, Wendell drops the friendly mask, revealing he is bound to the thing in the lake as its collector, and that Xanthe's childhood friendship was surveillance. Time limit stated plainly: seven days until the taker dies and takes the town's memories with it — including Xanthe's. Emotional beat: the wound of learning love was instrumentation.

chapters.title: The Missing Yearbook
chapters.summary: At the county library, Xanthe confirms the erasure mechanically: the 1974 yearbook page is razored out, the class photo reprinted without a gap, and the librarian who notices the gap forgets it within minutes while talking to him. Emotional beat: horror of institutionalized forgetting; identity as something administratively deletable.

chapters.title: Caller Number Nine
chapters.summary: A live caller, a woman in her fifties, remembers a brother she was told never existed — Toby — and the memory is physically painful for her, bleeding her nose mid-call. The dead callers chant his name softly beneath hers. Emotional beat: hope that memory can be recovered, at cost.

chapters.title: Prewitt's Bargain
chapters.summary: Prewitt invites Xanthe to dinner and confesses partially: the founding families traded a child's existence for the reservoir's endless clean water and the town's survival through the '74 drought. He urges Xanthe to let the debt lapse — the forgetting will simply become permanent and painless. Emotional beat: seductive power of comfortable complicity.

chapters.title: The Drowned District
chapters.summary: Diving with borrowed equipment near the old church steeple visible in drought-low water, Xanthe finds the Vance house foundation and, wedged in the silt, a child's shoe and a nameplate. Something vast turns over below him. Emotional beat: awe and terror; the lake is not empty.

chapters.title: Seven Callers
chapters.summary: The show is hijacked: seven dead voices speak simultaneously through the board, reciting fragments of Toby's life until the transmitter burns out. Station manager fires Xanthe on the spot, then forgets him entirely by the time he reaches the parking lot. Emotional beat: isolation deepening — the erasure is beginning to eat him too.

chapters.title: What Wendell Was For
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, nine-year-old Xanthe's POV in summer 1974: Wendell led him to the creek, to Toby, to the game they played — and away, on the crucial afternoon, so the adults could do what they did. Emotional beat: devastating retroactive understanding of his own complicity.

chapters.title: The Founders' Meeting
chapters.summary: Xanthe breaks into the Harrow Bend historical society and finds the original covenant signed by nine families, each signature accompanied by a lock of hair — one bundle labeled V., its hair still wet fifty years on. Prewitt catches him; the other founders arrive. Emotional beat: cornered; power showing its face.

chapters.title: They Take His Voice
chapters.summary: The founders perform a minor rite stripping Xanthe's ability to say the name — the word dissolves on his tongue. They explain, almost kindly, that power requires maintenance, and maintenance requires silence. Wendell watches from the doorway and does nothing. Emotional beat: helplessness and rage.

chapters.title: The Mother's Voice
chapters.summary: His dead mother calls the station's ruined line directly to Xanthe's cell: she resisted in 1974, hid the tape, and tells him the name needn't be spoken by him — only returned by love, aloud, at the water. She gives him the last piece: Toby's full name and the lullaby she sang to both boys. Emotional beat: posthumous maternal love as the counter-power.

chapters.title: Wendell's Choice
chapters.summary: Xanthe confronts Wendell with the flashback truth; Wendell, tormented, admits he was once a real child taken first, reshaped into the collector. He can unlock Xanthe's voice by giving up his form. Emotional beat: pity replacing hatred; the corrupted are also victims of power.

chapters.title: Night of the Rising Water
chapters.summary: The founders, sensing the debt coming due, begin a counter-rite to renew the bargain using a new child — Prewitt's grandson. Xanthe races the ritual through streets filling with lake water that behaves like memory, flooding residents with everything they forgot. Emotional beat: escalating chaos, the town drowning in itself.

chapters.title: The Church Below
chapters.summary: Climax: in the submerged church, Xanthe — voice restored by Wendell's sacrifice, the boy collapsing into a middle-aged stranger weeping — sings his mother's lullaby and speaks Tobias Ellery Vance aloud into the water. The thing beneath rises, is named, and cannot hold a named shape; the covenant burns. Emotional beat: terrible release.

chapters.title: What the Water Gave Back
chapters.summary: Dawn: the reservoir recedes unnaturally, exposing the old district. Residents wander the ruins remembering, some kneeling at the Vance house foundation. The founders age decades in minutes as their stolen vitality returns to the town. Prewitt, broken, thanks him. Emotional beat: mourning and restitution entangled.

chapters.title: Toby
chapters.summary: At the restored grave — new stone, old dates — Xanthe meets the man Wendell became, ordinary and grieving, who remembers being two boys at once. They bury the striped scarf together. Emotional beat: quiet reconciliation with the self he was.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: Final broadcast: Xanthe opens the lines and the first caller is living — a Vance cousin who found the family Bible with a new inked entry. He signs off with his mother's sign-off phrase, and for the first time in twenty years, sleeps before dawn. Emotional beat: earned peace, identity reclaimed through witness.
